blocks.text: Safe and responsible digital practice means using technology wisely and protecting personal information online: strong passwords, up-to-date software and avoiding unsafe websites (Fig 9.2). These habits prevent data loss, hacking and identity theft, so users enjoy technology without unnecessary risk and help build a secure, trusted digital environment.

blocks.title: Do you know?
blocks.text: A strong 12-character password could take a computer millions of years to crack, but a weak one can be cracked in seconds.
Online safety

Online safety means protecting yourself and your information on the Internet: being careful what you share, where you click and how you store data. Online actions leave digital footprints that can be tracked, so staying alert helps avoid scams, viruses and other threats and keeps personal and school data secure.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Understanding threats and how to prevent them reduces the chance of cybercrime.
Strong passwords

A strong password combines upper- and lower-case letters, numbers and symbols, and is hard to guess. Use a different password for each account, avoid personal details such as names or birthdays, and never share them. A strong password is the first line of defence for your files and accounts.
Risky downloads and unsafe browsing

Files or programs from unknown websites can hide viruses or spyware that harm the computer or collect data without permission. Visiting fake websites or clicking unknown links can lead to scams or identity theft. Check sources before downloading and use antivirus tools for extra protection.
Software maintenance and updates

Software maintenance means keeping programs working well by updating them regularly. Updates fix errors, improve performance and close security gaps that hackers could exploit. Outdated software is an easy target: old versions may have known security holes, cause compatibility problems and raise the risk of malware and data breaches, so regular updates keep systems safe and dependable.

blocks.title: Class activity
blocks.text: Compare the features of updated and outdated software, and discuss how old versions can be attacked.
Privacy and security settings

Privacy and security settings, found in most apps and websites, let users control how their personal information, such as location, contacts and browsing history, is used and shared. On Instagram, for example, a user can make the account private so only approved followers see posts, turn off location sharing and turn on two-factor authentication. On WhatsApp, users can choose who sees their profile photo (everyone, only contacts or nobody) and can turn off read receipts (the blue ticks). Settings should be reviewed regularly, because platforms change their features and rules.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Reviewing settings regularly keeps you protected as platforms update their features.
Reading privacy policies

A privacy policy explains how a website or app collects, stores, uses and shares your data. Read it before creating an account or accepting the terms: when signing up to a social platform, the policy says what may be collected (name, email address, location, browsing activity, app usage) and whether it is shared with advertisers or third parties. This lets you decide whether to share your data.
Safe online collaboration

Online collaboration lets people work together from anywhere using digital tools, so use secure platforms and follow safety rules when sharing files. Secure platforms such as Google Workspace and Microsoft Teams use encrypted communication and access controls. For a group project in Google Docs, share the file only with trusted classmates through restricted access, and give 'View only' rather than 'Edit' to those who only need to read it; online classes on Google Meet can admit only authorised participants.
Digital etiquette

Digital etiquette means communicating politely, respectfully and clearly online: appropriate language, respect for others' opinions, no sharing of private information and no misuse of tools. In a class group chat, avoid spam, unrelated memes or jokes during serious discussions, so the group stays useful and focused on learning.

blocks.alt: A checklist of six safe habits, each with a tick: strong, unique passwords (12 or more characters; letters, numbers, symbols; one per account); keep software updated; download only from trusted sources; check privacy settings; turn on two-factor authentication; think before you share or click. A side box contrasts a weak made-up password (ali2008: name and birth year, short) with a strong one (Kite!Rain7-Chai*Lake: long, mixed, nothing personal).
